Accountability · Asylum spending · Opinion

Smash the gangs? Not in our plans.

Labour promises a crackdown. Its asylum spending and accommodation plans stretch years into the future.

Steve English · 18 October 2026

Labour promises the British public it will “smash the people-smuggling gangs”. Yet its own asylum budgets and accommodation plans prepare for provision stretching well into the next decade.

Taxpayers hear promises of a crackdown. They deserve to know when that will translate into lasting results—and how many more billions they will be expected to pay along the way.

BILLIONS NOW. MORE YEARS OF BILLS AHEAD.

The current asylum accommodation contracts run from 2019 to 2029. Originally expected to cost £4.5 billion, their estimated total cost has ballooned to £15.3 billion.

That is more than three times the original estimate.

Labour inherited those contracts from the Conservatives. But in April 2025, under Labour, the Home Office also awarded a £550 million, four-year contract for contingency hotel accommodation.

These are whole-contract figures, covering their full terms—not annual bills or amounts all still to be spent.

NOW LOOK AT THE SPENDING PLANS

The government’s 2025 Spending Review figures imply asylum spending of approximately £3.6 billion in 2026–27, £2.9 billion in 2027–28 and £2.5 billion in 2028–29.

Around £9 billion across three financial years. Taxpayers’ money.

Those forecasts cover asylum spending more broadly than accommodation alone. They overlap with contract spending, so they must not be added to the contract totals. But they show the scale of the bill ministers still expect.

AND WHAT IF THIS BILL BALLOONS TOO?

The existing accommodation contracts were supposed to cost £4.5 billion. Their estimated cost has swollen to £15.3 billion.

What if the £9 billion spending forecast overshot by the same proportion? The bill would reach roughly £30 billion.

That is a warning scenario, not a forecast: the figures cover different things and different periods. But after one estimate more than tripled, taxpayers have every reason to demand evidence that ministers can keep the next bill under control.

AND WHAT HAPPENS AFTER 2029?

The Home Office is preparing replacement asylum accommodation arrangements starting in September 2029, running to 2036, with a possible extension to 2039.

Another thirteen years from today.

These national arrangements are proposed, rather than signed contracts. Nevertheless, they reveal the timescale the government is putting before suppliers.

In September 2026, the government told Parliament that its replacement contracts would ensure the “continuous delivery of asylum accommodation” from September 2029 onwards.

The existing contracts take us to 2029. The replacement plans could take us another decade beyond that.

WHERE IS THE TIMETABLE FOR SUCCESS?

The government says it must replace expiring contracts and meet its legal obligations. Asylum accommodation also serves people who did not arrive in small boats. Contract dates alone cannot prove how many illegal crossings ministers expect in 2039.

But taxpayers are entitled to ask how this long-term planning fits with the impression of decisive action Labour sells to the public.

When does Labour expect its crackdown to produce a lasting reduction in illegal crossings? How much accommodation will it need afterwards? Will the replacement contracts allow capacity—and costs—to fall if its policies succeed?

“Smash the gangs” is a slogan. Taxpayers deserve measurable results, a deadline and an explanation of what happens to these arrangements when ministers deliver what they promise.

It is easy to make promises when somebody else pays for failure.
